newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala eyes to expand hedged coffee loan scheme.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala eyes to expand hedged coffee loan scheme.

text.p: The National Coffee Association (Anacafe) wants to expand a hedged loan program in which coffee growers commit to selling their beans at or above a certain price, Anacafe's president said Thursday.
"To receive this financing, the producer must fix a minimum price for the coffee so if the market drops, this (set) price will cover the loan," Max Quirin told Reuters in an interview.

Quirin said during the first two years of the program, large and small coffee producers have received $20 million in loans but Anacafe wants to expand the program to $200 million in loans to cover the financial needs of the entire sector.

Under the program so far, Guatemalan banks have been giving one-year loans at 13 to 14 percent interest rates, but Anacafe is seeking lines of credit from foreign banks and hoping to expand terms to two-to-three years.
Quirin said the loan program is more practical than an innovative measure Guatemala coffee producers launched three years ago: coffee bonds.
In 1993, Guatemala issued $60 million in coffee bonds through the Bank of New York to finance producers in a period low coffee prices at the time, said Quirin.

Producers throughout Guatemala benefited from the sale of the five-year bonds with an 11 percent interest rate. Anacafe collects regular contributions from the growers to make payments to a trust that pays interest to the bond holders.

According to Quirin Guatemalans bought half the bonds and the other half were sold internationally and he added the outstanding debt on the bonds is down to $36 million because coffee producers have already bought back $24 million.

Quirin said the bonds are currently trading at 100 percent face value. A year after launch, he said the bonds fell to 98 percent of face value but then recovered. At one point, they reached a high of 104 percent.
